pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Ohm's Law: voltage, current, resistance

- **Standards:** This topic STRADDLES KS3→KS4 (UK); it is UK-anchored for the US.

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum):** KS3 'Current electricity' defines resistance as 'measured in ohms, as the ratio of potential difference (p.d.) to current', which is exactly R = V/I and licenses rearranging it — so the CALCULATION sits within KS3 reach; however the NAME 'Ohm's Law' appears NOWHERE in the National Curriculum at either key stage (it is a textbook/exam-board convention), and the GRAPHICAL exploration of current–voltage relationships for different components (I–V characteristics) is KS4 'exploring current, resistance and voltage relationships for different circuit elements, including their graphical representations' (all verified by fetch). So: the V=IR ratio and calculation = KS3; the named law and I–V graphs = KS4.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** no middle-school PE covers DC-circuit resistance/Ohm calculations, so this is UK-anchored.

- **Operational details:** This is a PROCEDURAL topic: given two of voltage, current and resistance, the child applies V = IR, rearranges it for the unknown, and explains that resistance OPPOSES current, naming the factors that change it (material, length, thickness). It builds directly on the previous topic's meanings of V and I; the new object is resistance, R, as the ratio that links them. The best teaching keeps the algebra tethered to meaning — resistance is how hard the circuit makes it for charge to flow, so for a fixed push (V) more resistance means less current, and for a fixed resistance more push means more current — rather than letting the formula triangle become a meaningless symbol-shuffle. A particle picture of resistance (charge colliding with a lattice; a longer wire = more collisions; a thicker wire = more lanes) makes the factors causal rather than memorised.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal-operational / quantitative, ~12–13).
bestPractices: Build V = IR FROM the ratio definition the child already met: resistance is potential difference divided by current (R = V/I), so V = IR and I = V/R are the same relationship rearranged — derive it, don't drop it as a triangle.

Teach resistance as OPPOSITION to flow with a causal picture: charges collide with the vibrating lattice of the material; more collisions = more resistance = less current for the same voltage. This makes 'opposes current' mechanistic, not a slogan.

Make the factors predictable from the picture: a LONGER wire = more collisions on the way = more resistance; a THICKER wire = more parallel lanes = less resistance; different MATERIALS pack the lattice differently. Have pupils predict before checking.
Drill the proportional reasoning, not just substitution: for fixed R, doubling V doubles I; for fixed V, doubling R halves I. The relationships matter more than the arithmetic at this tier.

Use the formula triangle ONLY as a support after meaning is secure, and warn against it as a crutch — require a sentence of reasoning ('more resistance, same push, so less current') alongside any rearrangement.

Keep 'resistance opposes / reduces current' distinct from 'resistance uses up current' — resistance lowers the rate of flow everywhere in a series loop; it does not consume charge (the current is still the same all the way round, just smaller).

Flag honestly that real components aren't all 'ohmic': a filament bulb's resistance rises as it heats, so V and I are not simply proportional — but the graphical I–V treatment of that is the KS4 extension, kept qualitative here.
keyRepresentations: The ratio/relationship trio R = V/I, V = IR, I = V/R — shown as rearrangements of ONE relationship, each readable in words ('current is push divided by opposition').
Particle model of resistance — charges colliding with a lattice; longer wire = more collisions, thicker wire = more lanes, making the factors causal.
The V–I proportional relationship for a fixed resistor — double the voltage, double the current — introduced numerically/in words (the formal straight-line graph is the KS4 step).
The formula triangle (V over I and R) — a calculation support, explicitly labelled a crutch to be backed by reasoning.
A variable circuit picture — a battery slider (V) and a resistor slider (R) with a live ammeter (I) showing how changing one moves the current.
commonMisconceptions: Treating V = IR as a meaningless triangle to shuffle — substituting without knowing which quantity is the push, the flow, or the opposition.
Thinking resistance 'uses up' current — resistance REDUCES the current (everywhere in a series loop) but does not consume charge; the current is still the same all the way round, just smaller.
Believing a thicker wire has MORE resistance — it has LESS (more lanes for charge); thickness and length pull opposite ways.
Assuming current and voltage are always directly proportional — only when resistance is constant; a heating filament's resistance rises, so its V–I line bends (the KS4 caveat).
Confusing which quantity changes when — e.g. expecting changing the resistor to change the battery's voltage; the cell sets V, the circuit's R then sets I.
Mis-rearranging the equation — e.g. writing I = VR instead of I = V/R — from manipulating symbols without the proportional sense (more opposition must mean less current).
Equating 'Ohm's Law' with all components — it describes the constant-resistance (ohmic) case; not every component obeys a single straight-line relationship.

learn.summary: For ages 12–13, Ohm's Law (V = IR) is taught as ONE relationship linking voltage (the push), current (the flow) and resistance (the opposition). Current is proportional to voltage only while resistance stays constant. The relationship is derived from the ratio definition R = V/I rather than memorised as a formula triangle. The core learning is seeing how current responds when you change voltage or resistance, and understanding WHY via a particle picture of charges colliding with the lattice: in a longer wire each charge meets more collisions along the way, and a thinner wire has fewer parallel lanes for charge, so both give more resistance. Activities cover an interactive sandbox for cause-and-effect exploration, a retrieval set for calculation fluency, reference supports, and a Socratic debrief. Note the UK curriculum placement: the V=IR ratio and calculation sit at KS3, while the named 'Ohm's Law' and graphical I–V treatment are KS4 extensions kept qualitative here.

activities.title: Ohm's Law sandbox: change the push, change the opposition
feedback: When the learner predicts the current wrongly on a voltage change, point back to the proportional link: same resistance, twice the push, so twice the flow.
If a learner expects a thicker wire to have more resistance, show the particle view — a thicker wire offers more parallel lanes, so more charge gets through and resistance is lower.
Reinforce that the current still flows everywhere in the loop, just at a smaller rate: resistance reduces the flow, it does not use up or consume the charge.
If the learner assumes voltage and current are always proportional, use the filament mode to show the relationship bending once resistance changes with heating (kept qualitative; the graph is KS4).
Praise reasoning stated in words ('more opposition, same push, so less current') over silent slider-dragging.
activities.rationale: A manipulable sandbox with sliders and a live ammeter lets current respond to changes the learner makes, turning the equation from symbol-shuffle into observed proportional behaviour; the particle-view toggle supplies a mechanistic reason for the factor effects, and the optional filament mode previews the non-ohmic case. A fixed diagram can show the relationship but cannot let the learner test it interactively. This is a research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: The 'resistance uses up current', formula-triangle-without-meaning, and thicker-wire-more-resistance errors are documented difficulties best addressed by deriving V=IR from the ratio, drilling proportional reasoning, and a collision/particle picture of resistance and its factors.
learnerActions: Set a battery to 3 V across a resistor and read the current on a live ammeter.
Keeping the same resistor (constant resistance), drag the voltage to 6 V and watch the current double in real time — put twice the push in, get twice the flow.
Holding the voltage fixed, make the wire thicker and watch the current climb; lengthen it and watch the current fall.
Try a material swap to see that different materials give different resistance for the same size of wire.

Toggle a particle view that shows charges colliding with the lattice: observe that in a longer wire each charge meets more collisions along the way, and that a thinner wire has fewer parallel lanes for charge, so fewer charges get through per second.
Use a 'predict the ammeter, then reveal' mode: commit a value for the current before the meter is uncovered on each change.
Optionally switch on a filament mode where the resistance climbs as the wire heats, so the current no longer simply doubles when the voltage doubles — a qualitative preview of the KS4 non-ohmic case.
Read V = IR updating beside every move and say aloud which quantity is the push, which is the flow, and which is the opposition.
activities.intendedInsight: V = IR is a description of cause and effect the learner controls: for a fixed resistance, doubling the voltage doubles the current; for a fixed voltage, doubling the resistance halves the current. The factor effects (longer = more resistance, thicker = less resistance, material matters) become causal through the collision picture, not memorised. The optional filament mode shows that this neat proportionality holds only while resistance stays constant.

activities.title: Calculate and reason: V, I, R fluency set
feedback: For a rearrangement slip (multiplying when division is needed), have the learner re-derive from R = V/I and check against a proportional sentence.
If a learner picks I = VR, ask what should happen to current when resistance grows — the formula they chose makes current grow, which contradicts 'opposition reduces flow'.
When units are dropped, ask which quantity each number measures before accepting the answer.
activities.rationale: A scored, well-defined item set is a natural fit for checking calculation and rearrangement fluency and for surfacing the common errors. It verifies fluency but does not itself provide the manipulable experience of watching current respond, so it works best as a companion to the sandbox. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: The 'resistance uses up current', formula-triangle-without-meaning, and thicker-wire-more-resistance errors are documented difficulties best addressed by deriving V=IR from the ratio, drilling proportional reasoning, and a collision/particle picture of resistance and its factors.
learnerActions: Solve fill-in/numeric V=IR problems with friendly numbers: find I given V and R; find R given V and I; find V given I and R.
Answer proportional-reasoning questions such as 'voltage doubles, resistance stays the same — what happens to the current?' (it doubles).

Sort changes — longer wire / shorter wire / thicker wire / thinner wire — into 'more resistance' vs 'less resistance', and note that changing to a different material can give either more or less resistance depending on which material is used.
Spot the wrong rearrangement: identify that I = VR is incorrect and that I = V/R is right, explaining that more opposition must mean less current.
Write the correct unit beside each answer (volts, amperes, ohms) and say which unit belongs to which quantity.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can rearrange the single relationship for any unknown, attach correct units, and use proportional reasoning rather than rote substitution. Catching I = VR as wrong comes from the proportional sense, not from symbol-manipulation alone.

activities.title: Quick reference: the relationship and the particle picture
feedback: If a learner reaches for the formula triangle, require a sentence of reasoning alongside any rearrangement so the triangle stays a support, not a crutch.
activities.rationale: A tappable reference supports recall of symbols, units and factor effects. It cannot let current respond to a changed voltage or resistance, so it serves as reference beside the interactive work, not as the place where the proportional concept is first built. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
learnerActions: Tap each symbol in R = V/I / V = IR / I = V/R to reveal its quantity, unit and plain-words meaning ('current is push divided by opposition').
Tap a longer or thinner wire in a labelled diagram to reveal 'more resistance', and a thicker wire to reveal 'less resistance'.
Use the reference alongside the sandbox or the calculation set as a memory aid, not as the main teacher.
activities.intendedInsight: The three forms R = V/I, V = IR and I = V/R are rearrangements of ONE relationship, each readable in words; the factor effects can be recalled with a labelled picture.

activities.title: Engineer debrief: what happens to the current if...?
feedback: Press for the mechanism: 'because resistance is opposition, halving it at the same voltage lets twice as much charge through per second, so the current doubles.'
If the learner says a big resistor stops current entirely, show that a large resistor still passes a small current — it reduces, not blocks.
activities.rationale: A Socratic dialogue can probe and firm up reasoning after hands-on exploration, targeting the specific misconceptions. Talk alone does not let the learner manipulate voltage or resistance or watch the current respond, so it works best as a debrief around the sandbox rather than as the primary teaching of the quantitative relationship. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
learnerActions: Respond to an engineer persona posing 'what happens to I if...' scenarios (e.g. 'you halved the resistance — what should the current do, and why?').
Explain the reason behind each prediction, not just the direction of change.
Correct, with guidance, the triangle-shuffle habit and the 'thicker wire = more resistance' error when they arise.
Articulate that resistance opposes and reduces current everywhere in a series loop but does not consume the charge.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can reason aloud about proportional changes and defend why, cementing 'resistance opposes, not consumes' and the inverse factor links.

constraints: Derive V = IR from the ratio definition the learner already met (R = V/I); do not introduce the formula triangle before meaning is secure, and when used require a sentence of reasoning alongside any rearrangement.
Keep 'resistance opposes/reduces current' distinct from 'resistance uses up current': current is the same all the way round a series loop, just smaller — charge is not consumed.
A large resistor reduces current but does not stop it entirely; a small current still flows.
Length and thickness pull opposite ways: longer wire = more resistance; thicker wire = less resistance. Do not conflate them.

Current and voltage are directly proportional ONLY when resistance is constant; a heating filament's resistance rises so its V–I line bends. Keep this qualitative — the graphical I–V treatment is a KS4 extension.

The static reference and the retrieval set are supports/checks: the reference cannot show current responding to change, and recognition/scored items verify fluency but do not by themselves provide the manipulable, mechanistic experience the sandbox gives.

Curriculum placement (UK): the V=IR ratio and calculation sit at KS3; the named 'Ohm's Law' and graphical I–V characteristics are KS4. There is no equivalent middle-school NGSS performance expectation, so this content is UK-anchored.

Interactive examples (sliders, live ammeter, particle-view toggle, material swap, filament mode, predict-then-reveal) are illustrative of the learning mechanism, not mandatory mechanisms or specific products.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The IOP Spark source backing the misconception/remediation claim is marked verified:false in the source row; treat its support as unconfirmed.

The source row framed a fixed page as something that 'cannot teach' the proportional core and stated '3D adds nothing' and 'weakly served by talk'; these comparative/necessity efficacy claims are not established by the evidence here and have been softened to scoped affordances/limits (interactive manipulation lets current respond; a static reference supports recall; dialogue does not provide manipulation).
Checked the worked examples: (a) R = V/I = 6/2 = 3 Ω; (b) I = V/R = 3/12 = 0.25 A; (c) doubling length doubles resistance so current halves (0.5 A → ~0.25 A). These are consistent.

The assessment's part (b) uses 3 V across 12 Ω giving 0.25 A, while part (c) describes a wire carrying 0.5 A at 4 V — ensure learners are not confused by the reused 0.25 A value across different scenarios; both are internally correct.

probeDeeper: Talk me through how you got from V = IR to your formula for R — why does R end up on its own like that?
In part (b) you got 0.25 A. If I doubled the voltage to 6 V, what would the current be, and why?
Would a thick copper wire or a thin copper wire of the same length have more resistance — and what would that do to the current?
What are the units of each of your answers, and how do you know which unit goes with which?
assess.correctAnswer: (a) R = V/I = 6/2 = 3 Ω. (b) I = V/R = 3/12 = 0.25 A. (c) Doubling the length doubles the resistance, so for the same 4 V the current halves — to about 0.25 A (it goes down).

errorPatterns.pattern: Rearrangement slip: computes R = V×I, or I = R/V — muddles the formula triangle rather than isolating the unknown correctly.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold with the V=IR triangle or a worked cover-up method, then have them re-derive R and I; check they can do the non-memorised rearrangement.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The written steps show the wrong operation (multiplying when division is needed), even though the child can state 'V = IR'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Resistance as a stopper: 'resistance stops the current — a big resistor means no current flows at all', so part (c) gives zero or 'none'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe resistance as opposition that reduces flow, tied to what current is (rate of charge flow); show a large resistor still passes a small current.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In part (c), or when asked what resistance does, predicts current is blocked entirely rather than reduced.

errorPatterns.pattern: Inverse-relationship error for resistance factors: thinks a longer (or thinner) wire lets MORE current through, or that doubling the length doubles the current.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the chain — longer wire → more resistance → (same V) less current; test with two wire lengths to make the inverse link concrete.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Part (c): predicts the current rises, or scales it the same way as the length instead of inversely.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot rearrange V = IR; multiplies when it should divide; or says a big resistor stops the current entirely.
responseLevels.full: Rearranges V = IR fluently with correct units and reasons about the relationship — doubling voltage doubles current, doubling length halves it — explaining resistance as opposition that reduces (not stops) current, and transferring to an unfamiliar variation.
responseLevels.partial: Substitutes and rearranges correctly for straightforward numbers and gives units, but stumbles when a factor changes (length or thickness) or when the required rearrangement isn't the memorised one — treating V = IR as a plug-in rule rather than a relationship.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these three on paper while I watch — show your steps and your units. (a) A 6 V battery drives 2 A through a lamp; find its resistance. (b) A 12 Ω resistor has 3 V across it; find the current through it. (c) A wire carries 0.5 A when 4 V is applied. You swap it for a wire of the same metal and thickness but twice as long — will the current go up or down, and roughly to what? Talk me through nothing in advance; just work, and I'll ask afterwards.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the working, not a description of it, reveals whether the child genuinely rearranges V = IR (rather than reciting it), tracks units, and treats resistance as opposition that reduces current. Rearrangement slips (multiplying instead of dividing), dropped units, and the 'longer wire lets more current through / resistance stops current' errors surface in the paper, where a verbal account would hide them.

sources.claim: KS3 defines resistance as 'measured in ohms, as the ratio of potential difference (p.d.) to current' (i.e. R = V/I); the phrase 'Ohm's Law' does not appear in the National Curriculum at any key stage, and the graphical current–voltage (I–V) treatment of different components is KS4 ('exploring current, resistance and voltage relationships for different circuit elements, including their graphical representations').
